<reason>Both sides executed at a high level with clean A1/A2 and Q1/Q2 compliance. Side A (CON) ran a disciplined textual strategy: the dilemma over who adjudicates "strongly shaped," the two-tier market, and the "shrinkage" narrative claiming PRO's exit right collapsed into CON's recalibration program. But that narrative overstates the retreat: PRO's conditional reading — refuse contaminated ratings, platform must then justify adverse action on checkable evidence — was on the table from the opening (B1.5), is the natural reading of the motion as written, and gave real content to the "strongly shaped" threshold under direct pressure (B4.1–B4.4). Meanwhile PRO landed the debate's strongest substantive blow: averaging stabilizes systematic bias rather than washing it out, which CON's "substitutes inherit bias with smaller samples" response only partially absorbed, especially after CON itself adopted telemetry and substantiated-complaint alternatives. PRO's convergence argument — that CON's endorsed burden-shifted appeals, audits, and weighting concede the premise that raw sentiment cannot end a livelihood — was accurate and forced the dispute onto favorable ground: who owns the remedy (right vs. favour). CON's "judge the words on the page" closing was crisp but formal, since PRO had defended those words plausibly. Honest concessions under pressure (B4.3) and the sustained "price on submission" framing give PRO the clearer path to victory, though CON's textual pressure keeps it competitive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B2.3–B2.4 reversal of CON's "thousands of customers whose outliers cancel out": distinguishing random noise from systematic bias and arguing that large samples perfect a biased instrument rather than rescue it. CON's A2.3 counter (bias runs through substitutes with smaller samples) was competent but was undermined when CON later listed checkable replacement metrics — PRO's B4.5 convergence claim then converted CON's own repair program into evidence for the motion.</best_rebuttal>
